name: Robert Williams
chief_complaint: Feeling tired and thirsty for the past 3 months
opening_statement: Hi doctor, I've been feeling quite tired lately and I'm always thirsty. My wife noticed I've been going to the bathroom a lot more at night, and I've lost about 5 kilos without trying. I'm a bit worried about what might be going on.
emotional_baseline: Concerned but cooperative. Appears motivated to understand his condition and willing to engage in management discussions.

symptoms.character: Passing urine 6-8 times during the day and waking 3-4 times at night to urinate

rag_citation.reference: Classic triad: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss. Polyuria occurs when plasma glucose exceeds renal threshold (~10 mmol/L)

symptoms.character: Drinking 3-4 litres of water daily, constant dry mouth

rag_citation.reference: Polydipsia is a compensatory mechanism for osmotic diuresis caused by hyperglycaemia

symptoms.character: 5 kg weight loss despite normal appetite

rag_citation.reference: Weight loss in uncontrolled diabetes results from glycosuria (loss of calories) and catabolism of fat and protein stores

symptoms.character: Generalised tiredness, lacking energy for usual activities

rag_citation.reference: Fatigue in diabetes relates to cellular energy deficit from insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency

symptoms.character: Difficulty reading small print, vision seems to fluctuate

rag_citation.reference: Hyperglycaemia causes osmotic changes in lens leading to refractive errors and blurred vision

past_medical_history.notes: Diagnosed 1 year ago, currently on perindopril 4mg daily, average BP 135/85 mmHg

family_history: Father had type 2 diabetes diagnosed at age 58, managed with tablets. Mother has hypertension. No family history of cardiovascular disease, thyroid disorders, or malignancy.

social_history.occupation: Office manager - sedentary job, sits 8-10 hours daily
social_history.alcohol: Social drinker - 2 standard drinks on weekends
social_history.exercise: Minimal - walks dog 15 minutes daily only
social_history.diet: Typical Australian diet - high carbohydrate intake, regular soft drinks, takeaway 2-3 times weekly
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife and two adult children, supportive family environment
social_history.functional_status: Independent in all ADLs, able to work full-time

examination_findings.general: Overweight male, appears well, no acute distress
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Heart sounds dual, no murmurs, peripheral pulses palpable bilaterally
examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly, no masses
examination_findings.neurological: Alert and oriented, cranial nerves intact, peripheral sensation grossly intact to light touch, ankle reflexes present
examination_findings.feet: No ulcers, calluses, or deformities noted on brief inspection

expected_management.action: Explain diagnosis of type 2 diabetes, pathophysiology, and importance of glycaemic control in preventing complications
expected_management.rationale: Informed patients have better adherence and outcomes

rag_citation.reference: Patient education is fundamental to diabetes self-management and should cover disease process, monitoring, lifestyle, and complication prevention

expected_management.action: Refer to accredited practising dietitian (APD) for individualised meal planning, recommend Mediterranean-style diet, target weight loss of 5-10%
expected_management.rationale: Lifestyle intervention is first-line for newly diagnosed T2DM

rag_citation.reference: Weight loss of 5-10% can significantly improve glycaemic control. Refer to APD for structured dietary advice

expected_management.action: Recommend 150 minutes moderate-intensity aerobic exercise weekly plus resistance training 2-3 times weekly. Consider exercise physiologist referral
expected_management.rationale: Exercise improves insulin sensitivity and cardiovascular fitness
expected_management.mbs_item: MBS Allied Health items under Team Care Arrangement

rag_citation.reference: Recommend at least 150 minutes/week moderate-intensity aerobic activity spread over at least 3 days, with resistance training 2-3 times weekly

expected_management.action: Initiate metformin 500mg daily with evening meal, titrate to 500mg BD after 1 week if tolerated, then to max dose 1000mg BD based on tolerance and HbA1c response
expected_management.rationale: Metformin is first-line oral hypoglycaemic agent unless contraindicated
expected_management.pbs_restriction: Unrestricted PBS benefit for type 2 diabetes

rag_citation.reference: Metformin is first-line pharmacotherapy. Start 500mg daily-BD with meals, increase gradually to 1000mg BD to minimise GI side effects

expected_management.action: Provide blood glucose meter and education on self-monitoring (fasting and 2-hour post-prandial initially). NDSS registration
expected_management.rationale: Self-monitoring enables patients to understand glycaemic patterns and treatment effects

rag_citation.reference: Register with NDSS for subsidised monitoring supplies. Self-monitoring frequency depends on treatment intensity

expected_management.action: Continue perindopril, consider statin therapy (atorvastatin 20mg) given dyslipidaemia and diabetes (high CVD risk). Aspirin not routinely recommended for primary prevention
expected_management.rationale: Diabetes confers high cardiovascular risk requiring aggressive lipid management
expected_management.pbs_restriction: Statins unrestricted PBS for diabetes patients

rag_citation.reference: Diabetes is considered high CVD risk. Statin therapy recommended for most adults with diabetes regardless of baseline lipids

expected_management.action: Arrange annual diabetic retinopathy screening (ophthalmologist/optometrist), comprehensive foot examination today and annually, baseline ACR and eGFR (already done)
expected_management.rationale: Early detection of microvascular complications enables timely intervention

rag_citation.reference: Screen for retinopathy, nephropathy (ACR/eGFR), neuropathy (foot examination) at diagnosis and annually thereafter

expected_management.action: Review in 2 weeks (medication tolerance, BGL patterns), then monthly until glycaemic targets achieved. Repeat HbA1c in 3 months. Target HbA1c ≤7% (53 mmol/mol)
expected_management.rationale: Close monitoring during treatment initiation ensures safety and efficacy

rag_citation.reference: Review HbA1c 3-monthly until stable, then 6-monthly. Target HbA1c ≤7% for most patients, individualised based on age and comorbidities

critical_errors.error: Failing to screen for diabetic retinopathy
critical_errors.consequence: Missed opportunity for early detection of vision-threatening retinopathy. Diabetic retinopathy can be asymptomatic until advanced stages.
critical_errors.reference: eTG requires retinal screening at diagnosis and annually - preventable blindness if missed

critical_errors.error: Prescribing metformin without checking renal function
critical_errors.consequence: Risk of metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA) if eGFR <30, dose adjustment needed if eGFR 30-45
critical_errors.reference: TGA warning - metformin contraindicated in severe renal impairment

critical_errors.error: Not providing patient education about hypoglycaemia recognition and management
critical_errors.consequence: Patient unprepared to recognise and treat hypoglycaemia, risk of severe events if occurs
critical_errors.reference: eTG - essential safety information for all diabetes patients on glucose-lowering therapy

critical_errors.error: Failing to register patient with NDSS (National Diabetes Services Scheme)
critical_errors.consequence: Patient misses subsidised access to blood glucose monitoring supplies, education resources, and support services
critical_errors.reference: NDSS registration provides substantial cost savings and support - standard of care in Australia

critical_errors.consequence: Patient unprepared for managing diabetes during intercurrent illness, risk of DKA/HHS
critical_errors.reference: eTG recommends sick day rules education at diagnosis

critical_errors.error: Failing to document target HbA1c and individualise based on patient factors
critical_errors.consequence: Unclear treatment goals, potential for over- or under-treatment
critical_errors.reference: eTG - individualised HbA1c targets based on age, comorbidities, hypoglycaemia risk

fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent representation of a straightforward new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in general practice. The persona appropriately reflects typical presentation with classic triad symptoms. Management plan is comprehensive and aligned with current eTG guidelines including appropriate use of MBS items for chronic disease management. Critical errors are well-chosen, particularly highlighting the importance of retinopathy screening and NDSS registration which are commonly overlooked. Difficulty calibration is appropriate for 'Easy' - single significant comorbidity (hypertension), straightforward diagnosis, no acute complications. RAG citations are accurate and confidence scores are realistic. This is examination-ready content.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACGP, GP with Special Interest in Diabetes, AMC examiner 8 years
fracp_reviews.comments: This persona accurately reflects a common general practice scenario that AMC candidates must be competent to manage. The opening statement is naturalistic and appropriate for the patient's age and background. Social history appropriately includes Australian-specific context (office manager occupation, typical diet patterns). Examination findings are realistic - mild hypertension despite treatment is common in newly diagnosed diabetics. The HbA1c of 7.8% is appropriate for a new diagnosis - high enough to require treatment but not so high as to suggest T1DM or acute metabolic decompensation. Management plan demonstrates comprehensive GP care including appropriate use of CDM plans (10950-10970) and annual cycle of care (10997) items. Critical error regarding metformin prescribing without renal function check is particularly important - this is tested in AMC exams. Lipid profile showing low HDL and high triglycerides (diabetic dyslipidaemia pattern) adds authentic complexity without increasing difficulty beyond 'Easy' level. Well-constructed persona.

learning_objectives.objective: Recognise classic presenting symptoms of type 2 diabetes mellitus (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue)
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Essential diagnostic skill - T2DM affects 1 in 20 Australians, early recognition enables timely intervention

learning_objectives.objective: Apply diagnostic criteria for type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≥6.5% or 48 mmol/mol, fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L)
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Accurate diagnosis using Australian guidelines (eTG) prevents both over- and under-diagnosis

learning_objectives.objective: Develop appropriate first-line management plan including lifestyle modification and metformin initiation
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Evidence-based pharmacotherapy reduces microvascular complications by 25% over 10 years (UKPDS)

learning_objectives.objective: Demonstrate appropriate use of Medicare Benefits Schedule items for chronic disease management (CDM plans, Team Care Arrangements, Annual Cycle of Care)
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Australian-specific healthcare system knowledge - enables multidisciplinary care coordination and subsidised allied health services

learning_objectives.objective: Identify mandatory screening requirements for diabetic complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) at diagnosis
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: 20% of patients have retinopathy at diagnosis - early detection prevents vision loss. Foot examination identifies high-risk feet requiring podiatry

learning_objectives.objective: Explain the importance of NDSS registration and patient education resources available in Australia
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: NDSS provides subsidised monitoring supplies saving patients $400-600 annually, plus evidence-based education programs improving outcomes

learning_objectives.objective: Assess cardiovascular risk in patients with diabetes and apply appropriate preventive strategies (statin therapy, blood pressure management)
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Cardiovascular disease causes 50% of deaths in diabetic patients - aggressive risk factor management reduces events by 33%

learning_objectives.objective: Formulate individualised HbA1c targets considering patient age, comorbidities, and hypoglycaemia risk
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Overly aggressive targets in older patients increase hypoglycaemia risk and mortality - personalised approach improves safety and adherence
